## Create a small data set

From the previous session on exploring data

```{r}
library(NHSRdatasets)

data <- NHSRdatasets::ae_attendances

smaller_data <- data |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1) |>
  dplyr::select(
    period,
    org_code
  )

# The data frame data
smaller_data

# The data frame with factor information
dput(smaller_data)
```

## Removing `factor`

To remove `factor` information we can create a new column (always a good idea in data analysis)

```{r}
add_to_data <- smaller_data |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Organisational code` = factor(org_code))

add_to_data
```

:::{.callout-tip collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
Notice the code creates a `tibble` when we've previously seen `data frame` when using base R.
:::

## Checking the structure

Let's check the structure again to see the difference between `Organisational code` and `org_code`

```{r}
str(add_to_data)
```

::: {.notes}
The use of a space in `Organisational code` is deliberate as this will be renamed in the next slide.

This replicates data as it often is written in Excel.

This is equivalent to the use of square brackets in SQL.
:::

## Rename a column using dplyr

Let's rename some more variables to something horrible:

```{r}
data_renamed <- data |>
  dplyr::rename(
    Breaches = breaches,
    PERIOD = period,
    ` type` = type
  )

data_renamed
```

## Little trick 

With the `dplyr::select()` function where you can select and rename in the same code

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::select(
    Breaches = breaches,
    PERIOD = period,
    ` type` = type
  )
```

## A quicker function using the `janitor` package

Notice it also cleans the leading whitespace which appears before the column name `type`

```{r}
janitor::clean_names(data)
```

## Over to you

Have a quick try at renaming breaches to 'no of breaches' then put it back again


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 5,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - renaming columns

```{r}
data_with_rename <- data |>
  dplyr::rename(`no of breaches` = breaches)

data_with_rename

colnames(data_with_rename)

data_with_rename <- data_with_rename |>
  dplyr::rename("breaches" = `no of breaches`)

data_with_rename
```

## janitor package and Excel

[`janitor`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/janitor/vignettes/janitor.html) has many useful functions to work with Excel including

::: {.incremental}
- Convert excel dates to dates (if they do that weird numeric thing)
- Find duplicate rows
- Add quick totals
:::

## `select()` refresher

From the [Introduction to R and R Studio course](https://intro-r-rstudio.nhsrcommunity.com/session-dplyr-showcase.html#/select) we learned 

::: {.incremental}
- selecting specific columns
- deselecting columns
- using the dplyr function `everything()`
- using dplyr functions `starts_with()`, `ends_with()` and `contains()`
:::

## Selecting by data type

It's possible to select columns by their data type using a base R function

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::select(where(is.numeric))
```


## Over to you

- Select the data so that the first column is `admissions`
- Then any column that is a factor 
- Followed by all the remaining columns


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 7,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - renaming columns

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::select(admissions, 
                where(is.factor), 
                dplyr::everything())
```
